Reproducing Semenov et al. (2026) from dandiset 001521¶

Paper: Semenov I, Silkuniene G, Silkunas M, Pakhomova ON, Bixler A, Ibey BL, Kochunov P, Pakhomov AG (2026). Sub-microsecond optical measurements of cell membrane charging and lesioning by pulsed electric fields. Bioelectrochemistry 171, 109283. doi:10.1016/j.bioelechem.2026.109283. The claims file was written from the version of record (main text with Materials and methods, figure legends and Data availability; the paper has no supplement and links no code).

Dandiset: DANDI:001521, version 0.261006.1845. The paper cites no version of the dandiset (its Data availability says data are available on request). This is the only published version, so it is pinned; the draft lists the same 73 assets with the same total size.

What the dandiset holds: 73 widefield Fluo-4 time-lapses of CHO cells (one NWB file each, no ROIs or traces), in two sessions. The 2025-02-03 session (31 files) is the single 1-us pulse experiment of Fig. 6A, and the 2025-05-02 session (42 files) is the 60-pulse 6 Hz train experiment of Fig. 6B. The pulsed-laser potentiometric imaging behind Figs. 1 to 5 and 7 is not in it. Six other dandisets of the same lab name the same paper (001515, 001516, 001517, 001518, 001525 and 001526); by their titles they hold the potentiometric experiments, and they are targets of their own.

Each file gives the pulse as a generator voltage, while the paper gives only field strengths. Two readings of the conversion are run throughout, and the one that fits the fields and group sizes of Fig. 6B is adopted (see "Field strengths"). The cell regions are found here by a standard segmentation, as the paper drew them by hand in MetaMorph (see fluo4.py).

No random numbers are drawn anywhere in this notebook.

Data check¶

Every file is streamed once and reduced, as it loads, to one background-corrected trace per cell (about four minutes). Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output.

The files hold one image series each and nothing else (no ROIs, traces, stimulus series or tables). The image unit is "n.a."; the values are raw camera counts (minimum 119, above the camera offset). The rates, frame counts and durations match the series descriptions and Methods 2.4: single pulses at 1 frame/s for 300 s with the pulse at 60 s; trains at 0.5 frame/s for 180 s with the train from 30 s (Methods: "a burst of 60 pulses at 6 Hz began at 30 s ... and recording continued for 150 s", 30 + 150 = 180 s). Every file states an electrode gap of 1.00 mm; the paper's Methods 2.2 give a 1.6 mm spacing. The dandiset's title and description mention only single pulses (next cell), but 33 of the 73 files are trains of 60 pulses; the other 9 files of the train session are shams. Every subject has an age of P1D, though subjects are fields of view of a cell line, and the species NCBITaxon 10029, which the archive's summary names "Cricetulus griseus - Cricetulus aureus", two species for one taxon (next cell).

The archive's metadata, for this dandiset and for the six other dandisets of the lab that name the same paper (each lists the paper's DOI as IsPublishedIn). By their titles the six hold the membrane polarization and recovery experiments; they are targets of their own and are not used here.

# Is a "subject" one cell, one dish or one field of view? Correlate the pre-pulse mean images.
Z = np.array([(r["pre_small"] - r["pre_small"].mean()).ravel() for r in res])
Z /= np.linalg.norm(Z, axis=1, keepdims=True)
C = Z @ Z.T
subj = info.subject_id.to_numpy(dtype=str)
same = subj[:, None] == subj[None, :]
off = ~np.eye(len(res), dtype=bool)
print(f"Correlation of pre-pulse images, files of the same subject: min {C[same & off].min():.3f}, "
      f"median {np.median(C[same & off]):.3f} ({(same & off).sum() // 2} pairs)")
print(f"Correlation of pre-pulse images, files of different subjects: max {C[~same].max():.3f}, "
      f"median {np.median(C[~same]):.3f}")
dups = [(info.path[i], info.path[j]) for i in range(len(res)) for j in range(i + 1, len(res))
        if np.array_equal(res[i]["pre_small"], res[j]["pre_small"])]
print("Pairs of files with identical pre-pulse images:", dups if dups else "none")
order = info.sort_values("session_start")
print("\nRecording order within each subject (voltages in order of session start):")
for s, g in order.groupby("subject_id", sort=False):
    print(f"  {s}: " + ", ".join(f"{v:.0f} V" for v in g.volts) + f"   cells per file {g.cells.tolist()}")

A subject is a field of view: the files of one subject show the same image (correlation 0.86 or more) and different subjects differ (0.43 at most). No file is a copy of another. Each field of view was recorded first without a pulse and then at escalating voltages, so the same cells were exposed up to seven times. For the trains this disagrees with Section 3.6 ("Each cell was tested only once"); for single pulses it agrees with the Results' "escalating field strengths". Cells are treated as independent across files of one field of view, as each recording has its own F0; results are broken down by field of view.

Of 608 objects, 76 were dropped (69 too small, 7 on the border). The single-pulse session holds 27 distinct cells in 6 fields of view (139 cell recordings); the paper averaged "across 14 cells" (Fig. 6A legend), which does not match either count, and the dataset does not say which 14. The train session holds 82 distinct cells in 9 fields of view (311 cell exposures to trains); the paper reports 224 cells, each tested once.

Without a pulse, dF falls steadily through the recording, to -12% (single-pulse session) and -16% (train session) over the last 10 frames, with F0 taken before the pulse as Methods 2.4 say. The next cell shows where the decline comes from.

In [8]:
# Where does the decline of unpulsed cells come from? Per set and voltage: the end value (last 10
# frames) relative to the pre-pulse mean of the background-corrected cell signal (dF), of the raw
# cell signal without background subtraction, of the cell-free background, and of the whole frame.
def rel_end(x, pf):
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    return 100 * (x[..., -fluo4.END_FRAMES:].mean(-1) / x[..., :pf].mean(-1) - 1)

rows = []
for s in ["single", "train"]:
    for v in sorted(info.volts[info.set == s].unique()):
        rs = [r for r in res if r["set"] == s and r["volts"] == v]
        pf = rs[0]["pulse_frame"]
        Fc = [r["F0"][:, None] * (1 + r["dF"] / 100) for r in rs]          # background-corrected F
        raw = [F + r["bg"][None] for F, r in zip(Fc, rs)]                   # F before background subtraction
        rows.append({"set": s, "volts": v, "files": len(rs), "cells": sum(len(F) for F in Fc),
                     "dF_end": np.concatenate([rel_end(F, pf) for F in Fc]).mean(),
                     "raw_cell_end": np.concatenate([rel_end(F, pf) for F in raw]).mean(),
                     "background_end": np.mean([rel_end(r["bg"], pf) for r in rs]),
                     "whole_frame_end": np.mean([rel_end(r["frame_mean"], pf) for r in rs]),
                     "background_over_F0": np.mean([r["bg"][:pf].mean() / r["F0"].mean() for r in rs])})
print("End value relative to the pre-pulse mean (%), by set and voltage:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2).to_string(index=False))

# Decline before the pulse (no pulse has yet been given in that recording), by recording order
# within the field of view: slope of each cell's dF over the pre-pulse frames, in % per minute.
rec = order.assign(order_in_fov=order.groupby("subject_id").cumcount() + 1)
pre = []
for i, r in enumerate(res):
    pf, t_min = r["pulse_frame"], np.arange(r["pulse_frame"]) / r["rate_hz"] / 60
    for c in range(len(r["dF"])):
        pre.append({"set": r["set"], "volts": r["volts"], "order_in_fov": int(rec.order_in_fov[i]),
                    "slope_pct_per_min": np.polyfit(t_min, r["dF"][c, :pf], 1)[0]})
pre = pd.DataFrame(pre)
print("\nPre-pulse slope of dF (% per min), by recording order within the field of view (1 = the sham):")
print(pre.groupby(["set", "order_in_fov"]).slope_pct_per_min.agg(["size", "mean", "sem"]).round(2).unstack(0).to_string())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3))
for ax, s in zip(axes, ["single", "train"]):
    rs = [r for r in res if r["set"] == s and r["volts"] == 0]
    pf, t = rs[0]["pulse_frame"], np.arange(rs[0]["shape"][0]) / rs[0]["rate_hz"]
    Fc = np.concatenate([r["F0"][:, None] * (1 + r["dF"] / 100) for r in rs])
    raw = np.concatenate([r["F0"][:, None] * (1 + r["dF"] / 100) + r["bg"][None] for r in rs])
    bg = np.array([r["bg"] for r in rs])
    for y, lab in [(Fc, "dF, background-corrected"), (raw, "raw cell signal"), (bg, "background")]:
        ax.plot(t, 100 * (y.mean(0) / y[:, :pf].mean() - 1), label=lab)
    ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.5, ls=":")
    ax.set_title(f"sham, {s} session ({len(Fc)} cells)", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("change from pre-pulse mean (%)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The decline is in the cells' own fluorescence, not in the background handling. In the sham recordings the raw cell signal, before any background is subtracted, falls by 8.7% (single) and 7.5% (train), while the cell-free background falls by 1.0% and 0.6%. Subtracting the background enlarges the relative decline (to -12.0% and -15.7%), because the background is 0.45 (single) to 1.26 (train) times the background-corrected cell signal; no choice of background region removes it, and dropping the subtraction, which Methods 2.4 prescribe, still leaves -8.7%. Fig. 6A of the paper shows the 0 V/cm mean trace rising to about +1% by 300 s, and the Fig. 6B traces are flat near zero, so the recordings or the processing behind the figure differ from these files in a way the paper does not describe (a question for the authors, see the summary).

The decline is also steepest in the first recording of a field of view and smaller in later ones: before the pulse, dF falls by 3.97% per minute in the first (sham) recording of the single-pulse session and by 1.46 to 0.41% per minute in the fifth to seventh; in the train session by 11.4% per minute in the first and 2.0 to 5.4% per minute later, without a steady trend after the first. As each field of view was recorded at escalating voltages, voltage and recording order go together, and any end value compared with the sham, which is always first, carries part of this difference. The step of dF at the pulse (shown for Fig. 6A below) does not.

# Does the response start at the stated pulse time? Step = mean dF over W frames after a putative
# pulse frame minus the W frames before it, strongly pulsed files minus sham files, with the
# putative pulse frame shifted.
def step(r, at, w):
    m = r["dF"].mean(0)
    return m[at:at + w].mean() - m[at - w:at].mean()

for s, strong, w in [("single", 350, 10), ("train", 230, 5)]:
    rs = [r for r in res if r["set"] == s]
    pf, n = rs[0]["pulse_frame"], rs[0]["shape"][0]
    shifts = np.arange(-pf + w, n - pf - w)
    contrast = [np.mean([step(r, pf + d, w) for r in rs if r["volts"] >= strong])
                - np.mean([step(r, pf + d, w) for r in rs if r["volts"] == 0]) for d in shifts]
    best = shifts[int(np.argmax(contrast))]
    rise = [int(np.argmax(np.diff(r["dF"].mean(0)))) + 1 for r in rs if r["volts"] >= strong]
    print(f"{s}: stated pulse at frame {pf} ({fluo4.PULSE_S[s]:.0f} s). Contrast (>= {strong} V minus sham) "
          f"at the stated frame {contrast[list(shifts).index(0)]:.2f}%, largest at shift {best:+d} frames "
          f"({max(contrast):.2f}%); at shifts -{w}, +{w}: "
          f"{contrast[list(shifts).index(-w)]:.2f}%, {contrast[list(shifts).index(w)]:.2f}%")
    print(f"   frame of steepest rise of the mean trace in the {len(rise)} files at >= {strong} V: "
          f"{sorted(rise)}")

single: stated pulse at frame 60 (60 s). Contrast (>= 350 V minus sham) at the stated frame 6.49%, largest at shift +1 frames (7.02%); at shifts -10, +10: 0.17%, 1.85%
   frame of steepest rise of the mean trace in the 7 files at >= 350 V: [40, 61, 61, 61, 67, 83, 249]
train: stated pulse at frame 15 (30 s). Contrast (>= 230 V minus sham) at the stated frame 79.10%, largest at shift +3 frames (146.56%); at shifts -5, +5: 1.57%, 116.57%
   frame of steepest rise of the mean trace in the 10 files at >= 230 V: [17, 18, 18, 18, 18, 19, 20, 20, 20, 33]

The recordings share the clock the descriptions give: the difference between strongly pulsed and sham files in the step of dF across a putative pulse frame is largest within one frame of the stated pulse for single pulses (frame 60 against 61), and three frames after the train onset for trains (the train lasts 10 s, five frames). With the pulse frame shifted 10 frames earlier (single) or 5 earlier (train), the contrast is near zero. This is a check of the stated timing against the responses; it is consistent with the data in both sessions.

Field strengths¶

The paper gives field strengths (Sim4Life values 5 um above the glass, Methods 2.2); the files give only the generator voltage, and neither states the conversion. Two readings are run (author, step 1.6):

  • M1, 3.9 V/cm per V, adopted as the main reading (an assumption, see below). The single-pulse voltages 150, 200, 250, 300 and 350 V then give 585, 780, 975, 1170 and 1365 V/cm, the field series the paper uses throughout (570, 780, 1000, 1200, 1400 V/cm), and the train voltages 70, 150, 170, 200, 230 and 250 V fall nearest the six fields labelled in Fig. 6B (230, 570, 650, 780, 900, 1000 V/cm).
  • M2, 3.3 V/cm per V, a variant. The train voltages 70, 200 and 230 V then give 231, 660 and 759 V/cm, the 230, 650 and 780 V/cm named for the trains in Section 3.6.

A field the paper names is assigned to the voltage whose field under the reading is nearest. Neither factor follows from the electrode gap (V/d is 10 V/cm per V for the 1.00 mm the files state and 6.25 V/cm per V for the 1.6 mm of Methods 2.2), as the paper's fields are simulated at the cells.

def group_table(d, value):
    """Per voltage: n, mean, s.e., one-sample t-test against 0 and Student's t-test against sham."""
    sham = d[d.volts == 0][value]
    rows = []
    for v, g in d.groupby("volts"):
        x = g[value]
        one = stats.ttest_1samp(x, 0)
        two = stats.ttest_ind(x, sham) if v != 0 else None
        rows.append({"volts": v, "n": len(x), "mean": x.mean(), "se": x.sem(),
                     "t_vs_0": one.statistic, "p_vs_0": one.pvalue,
                     "diff_vs_sham": x.mean() - sham.mean() if v != 0 else np.nan,
                     "p_vs_sham": two.pvalue if two else np.nan})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("volts")

Under M1 the six Fig. 6B fields take six different train voltages, and the dataset's group sizes are close to the figure's n (equal at 230 V/cm, and within 3 at 570, 650 and 1000 V/cm; larger at 780 and 900 V/cm). Under M2, 900 and 1000 V/cm fall on 250 and 300 V, and the 300 V group has 6 cells where the figure has 36; the six M2 groups happen to sum to 224, the paper's total, while the M1 groups sum to 256. The same electrodes and generator served both sessions (Methods 2.2), so M1 is adopted for both sessions, as an assumption; M2 is still shown for every claim. The train voltages 100, 180, 190, 210, 220 and 300 V are in no Fig. 6B group under M1.

fig6a-ca-entry-1000-1200¶

A single 1-us pulse causes clear Ca2+ entry into CHO cells at 1000 and 1200 V/cm, among field strengths escalated from 0 to 1200 V/cm.

Criterion (claims file): per cell dF as in Methods 2.4; reproduced when, under at least one reading, the post-pulse dF at both 1000 and 1200 V/cm is significantly above zero (one-sample t-test) or above the 0 V/cm group (two-tailed Student's t-test) at p < 0.05, and the group means at 1000 and 1200 V/cm exceed those of every field of 650 V/cm or less. The post-pulse value is read as (a) the mean of the last 10 frames or (b) each cell's peak after the pulse. Both conversions are run.

Result: reproduced, under both conversions. Under M1 (250 and 300 V), three of the four readings hold at both fields: the end value against the 0 V/cm group (p = 4.9e-09 and 3.0e-11), and the peak against zero or against the 0 V/cm group (means 2.30 and 5.35% against at most 0.55% at 650 V/cm or less). The end value against zero fails: it is below zero at both fields (-5.44 and -3.83%), as is the sham (-12.0%). Under M2 (300 and 350 V) the same three readings hold. In every field of view the peak at 250 V is above the peak at 0 V, and at 300 V above the peaks at 0 and 150 V. With fields of view as the unit, the peak less the same field of view's sham is 2.42% at 250 V (4 fields of view, p = 0.0004) and 5.02% at 300 V (5, p = 0.0002).

The end and peak readings compare later recordings with the sham, recorded first, while the decline is steepest in the first recording (data check). The step at the pulse, which that does not affect, is above the sham's at 250 V (0.35 +- 0.17%, against the sham p = 0.025) and 300 V (1.78 +- 0.31%, p = 3.2e-07), and not at 150 or 200 V (p = 0.13 and 0.10); at 250 V it is small and not above zero on its own (p = 0.058). The entry at 1000 V/cm under M1 is therefore a small one, a few tenths of a percent at the pulse, and clearer at 1200 V/cm (1.78%) and above (3.94% at 350 V). The single-pulse session holds 27 cells in 6 fields of view, and three sets of fields of view give 14 cells, so which 14 cells Fig. 6A averages cannot be told from the data.

Result: not reproduced, under both conversions. The end-of-recording dF is below zero at 1000 and 1200 V/cm under M1 (-5.44 and -3.83%) and at 1000 V/cm under M2 (-3.83%); at 1200 V/cm under M2 (350 V) it is +1.24% with p = 0.53. The final over peak ratio of the group mean trace is -63 and -2.4 under M1. The decline is the one the sham shows, and it is in the cells' raw fluorescence (-8.7% in the sham), not in the background (-1.0%), so it does not come from how the background was taken (data check). Against the 0 V/cm group the end value is higher by 6.6 and 8.2% (p = 4.9e-09 and 3.0e-11), and less the same field of view's sham trace it is above zero at every voltage of 200 V or more (4.8 to 12.9%, p below 0.001), but these comparisons include the change of the decline with recording order. So the signal stays above that of unpulsed cells to the end, but not above its own pre-pulse level, which is what the criterion tests. The paper's Fig. 6A shows no such decline in its 0 V/cm trace, so the outcome rests on a difference between these recordings and the figure that the paper does not explain.

Result: reproduced, under both conversions. The one-sample test finds no increase at 780 V/cm: the end value is -7.42 +- 0.52% under M1 (200 V, n = 24) and -5.44 +- 0.55% under M2 (250 V, n = 18), one-sided p = 1 for an increase in both. This test cannot detect an increase here: it also finds none at 1000 and 1200 V/cm under M1, where the end values are -5.44 and -3.83%. Of the variants, the end value against the 0 V/cm group (higher by 4.60%, p = 1.3e-06) and the peak (1.76 +- 0.61%, against zero p = 0.0086, against the sham peak p = 0.021) find an effect at 780 V/cm under M1, and both also carry the order effect of the data check. The step at the pulse, which separates 1000 and 1200 V/cm from the sham (p = 0.025 and 3.2e-07), finds none at 780 V/cm under M1 (0.15 +- 0.16%, p = 0.10); under M2, where 780 V/cm is 250 V, it finds one (0.35 +- 0.17%, p = 0.025). The step is the only variant not confounded by recording order, but it is weak evidence here: it separates 1000 V/cm from the sham only barely (p = 0.025, and p = 0.058 against zero), and the steps at 780 and 1000 V/cm under M1 (0.15 +- 0.16 and 0.35 +- 0.17%) do not differ (p = 0.40). The end and peak readings against the sham, which also separate 1000 and 1200 V/cm from it, find an effect at 780 V/cm. So the outcome follows the claims file's test, which says little here. A question on the criterion's test is asked of a reader (questions/001521.yaml).

fig6b-train-threshold¶

With trains of sixty 1-us pulses at 6 Hz (each cell tested once, 224 cells), a strong Ca2+ response occurs in 28% of cells at 780 V/cm and in nearly all cells at higher fields.

Criterion (claims file): a strong response is (a) an end-of-recording dF above the largest among the 0 V/cm (or lowest field) cells, or (b) above 3 s.d. of that group, read here as above its mean plus 3 s.d.; reproduced when, under one reading, the fraction at 780 V/cm is within 28 +- 2.8% and at least 90% respond at every field above 780 V/cm. Expected: 224 cells tested with trains.

        rows.append({"mapping": m, "rule": k, "V_780": v780, "pct_780": frac.loc[v780, k],
                     "in_tolerance": abs(frac.loc[v780, k] - 28) <= 2.8, "higher_V": higher,
                     "min_pct_higher": frac.loc[higher, k].min(), "all_higher_ge_90": (frac.loc[higher, k] >= 90).all()})
readings_6b = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(readings_6b.round(1).to_string())

Result: not reproduced. The fields above 780 V/cm are taken as those of Fig. 6B, 900 and 1000 V/cm (230 and 250 V under M1, 250 and 300 V under M2). With the criterion's end window of 10 frames, under no reading is the fraction at 780 V/cm within 25.2 to 30.8%: it is 2.9 to 22.1% under M1 (200 V, 68 cells) and 44.7 to 78.7% under M2 (230 V, 47 cells), over the six rules, including "above 3 s.d." read literally (a threshold of 3 s.d. of the reference group). Nor do 90% respond at both higher fields: the lower of the two fractions is 44.7 to 78.7% under M1 and 61.5 to 79.5% under M2. The six voltage groups that correspond to the Fig. 6B fields hold 256 cells under M1 and 224 under M2, against the paper's 224; in all, the dataset holds 311 cell exposures to trains, of 82 distinct cells, not 224 cells each tested once. Taking only the first train of each field of view, 9.1 to 18.2% respond at 200 V and 90.9 to 100% at 250 V (11 cells each). The region-size check below gives the same outcome in all 36 combinations, and so does a background less affected by dim cells. With an end window of 5 frames and a region of 0.5 of the radius, the 780 V/cm fraction under M1 and the rule "above the largest of the lowest field" is 27.9%, within tolerance, but the fields above it then reach 76.6% (230 V) and 82.1% (250 V), not 90%.

fig6b-650-weak-but-significant¶

With 60-pulse trains at 650 V/cm only 2 cells (5.9%) respond strongly, but the mean Ca2+ signal at the end of recording is significantly above zero and marginally above that at 230 V/cm.

Expected: 2 strongly responding cells, 5.9 +- 0.59%. The claim has no criterion of its own; a strong response is as in fig6b-train-threshold. The statement's tests (one-sample t-test against zero, p < 0.001; single-tailed t-test against 230 V/cm, p < 0.05) are run, with the direction of each effect.

Result: not reproduced. The statement's two tests fail under the adopted conversion and one fails under the other. Under M1 the mean end value at 170 V (650 V/cm) is -9.17 +- 0.83%, significantly below zero, not above it (one-sided p = 1 for above zero), and not above the 70 V group (single-tailed p = 0.20). Under M2 the 200 V mean is -1.98 +- 1.77%, not different from zero (p = 0.27), though above the 70 V group (single-tailed p = 0.0023). The expected count is met under one combination only: M1 (170 V, 36 cells), the rule "above the largest of the lowest field", and the region of 0.7 of the cell radius (2 cells, 5.6%); the other five rules give 0 cells under M1, regions of 0.5 and 1.0 of the radius give 1 cell (2.8%) under the same rule, and M2 (200 V, 68 cells) gives 2 to 15 cells (2.9 to 22.1%). As the tests fail under both conversions, the outcome does not depend on which conversion or rule is taken. The end values carry the decline of the data check.

Region size and end window¶

The region over each cell is 0.7 of the cell's equivalent radius (a standard choice), and the end value is the mean of the last 10 frames (the claims' criterion). The key numbers under regions of 0.5 and 1.0 of the radius and end windows of 5 and 20 frames, then every reading for the trains.

In [21]:
# Region size and end window are standard choices (claims file, opening comment): the key numbers under others.
def cells_for(roi, frames):
    out = []
    for i, r in enumerate(res):
        d = r["dF"] if roi == fluo4.ROI_FRACTION else r["dF_roi"][roi]
        out.append(pd.DataFrame({"set": r["set"], "volts": r["volts"], "end": fluo4.end_value(d, frames),
                                 "peak": fluo4.peak_value(d, r["pulse_frame"])}))
    return pd.concat(out, ignore_index=True)

rows = []
for roi in (0.5, fluo4.ROI_FRACTION, 1.0):
    for frames in (5, fluo4.END_FRAMES, 20):
        c = cells_for(roi, frames)
        a, b = c[c.set == "single"], c[c.set == "train"]
        sham_a = a[a.volts == 0].end
        sb, lb = b[b.volts == 0].end, b[b.volts == 70].end
        row = {"roi_fraction": roi, "end_frames": frames}
        for v in (0, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350):
            row[f"A_end_{v}V"] = a[a.volts == v].end.mean()
        for v in (250, 300):
            row[f"A_p_vs_sham_{v}V"] = stats.ttest_ind(a[a.volts == v].end, sham_a).pvalue
        for v in (300, 350):
            row[f"A_p_vs_0_{v}V"] = stats.ttest_1samp(a[a.volts == v].end, 0).pvalue
        for v in (170, 200, 230, 250, 300):
            x = b[b.volts == v].end
            row[f"B_pct_{v}V_a0"] = 100 * (x > sb.max()).mean()
            row[f"B_pct_{v}V_alow"] = 100 * (x > lb.max()).mean()
        row["B_n_strong_170V_alow"] = int((b[b.volts == 170].end > lb.max()).sum())
        rows.append(row)
robust = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(robust.round(3).T.to_string())

For single pulses the group end values move by less than 1% across these choices, and every comparison above keeps its direction and significance. For the trains, the fractions at 200 V under the rule "above the largest of the lowest field" range from 11.8 to 30.9%, and the count at 170 V from 0 to 3. One of these, the 5-frame window with a region of 0.5 of the radius, gives 27.9% at 200 V, within 28 +- 2.8%, but 76.6% at 230 V and 82.1% at 250 V, short of the 90% the criterion needs at the higher fields.

# Trains: every reading of the conversion, the response rule and the region size, with the end

rows = []

With the variant background, the background falls from 1.81 to 1.21 times the corrected cell signal in the train session (pre-pulse means over all train files), but the sham still declines, to -13.5% (train) and -11.3% (single), and the outcomes do not change: the fig6b-train-threshold criterion is met in none of the 12 combinations of conversion and rule (780 V/cm fraction 2.9 to 23.5% under M1 and 42.6 to 91.5% under M2, with the lower of the higher-field fractions at most 87.2%), the 650 V/cm mean stays below zero (-7.37% under M1, -1.54% under M2, one-sided p = 1.0 and 0.87 for above zero), and the count of 2 cells (5.9%) is met in none. So the dim cells inside the cell-free region do not decide these outcomes.

fig5b-conductivity-calibration¶

By Eq. 2, a 10-fold increase of effective membrane conductivity from 0.0003 mS/m reduces the pole IMP by only about 2%, and a 100-fold increase by 12%.

Criterion (claims file): a model computation with the paper's values (cytoplasm 0.4 S/m, medium 1.64 S/m, intact membrane 3e-7 S/m, R 8 um, d 5 nm). The reduction is 1 - f/1.5 (% of IMPC, Fig. 5B legend); f relative to f at the intact conductivity is a variant. Expected: 2 +- 0.2% and 12 +- 1.2%. This uses no recordings.

In [24]:
def f_eq2(lam_m, R=8e-6, d=5e-9, lam_i=0.4, lam_o=1.64):
    """Eq. 2 of the paper, with its constants (Methods 2.3)."""
    num = 3 * lam_o * (3 * R**2 * d * lam_i + (3 * d**2 * R - d**3) * (lam_m - lam_i))
    den = 2 * R**3 * (lam_m + 2 * lam_o) * (lam_m + 0.5 * lam_i) - 2 * (R - d)**3 * (lam_o - lam_m) * (lam_i - lam_m)
    return num / den

lam0 = 3e-7
rows = [{"fold": k, "lambda_m (S/m)": lam0 * k, "f": f_eq2(lam0 * k),
         "reduction_vs_IMPC_%": 100 * (1 - f_eq2(lam0 * k) / 1.5),
         "reduction_vs_intact_f_%": 100 * (1 - f_eq2(lam0 * k) / f_eq2(lam0))} for k in (1, 10, 100)]
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

The variant relative to the intact f gives 1.20 and 11.75%. This is a computation from the paper's equation and does not test the dataset.

21 claims on potentiometric imaging (Figs. 1 to 5 and 7) blocked: data missing

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's: the cell regions are found by a segmentation, not drawn by hand; the region size and the cell-free background region are standard choices; the voltages of the files are converted to field strengths at 3.9 V/cm per V (M1), an assumption that fits the fields and group sizes of Fig. 6B, with 3.3 V/cm per V (M2) shown throughout; all cells in every file are used, where the paper used 14 cells for Fig. 6A and 224 cells, each tested once, for Fig. 6B; the tests the paper does not name are the claims file's readings. No outcome changes between M1 and M2.

What was found about the dataset: it holds the Fluo-4 imaging of Fig. 6 and none of the potentiometric imaging; it gives voltages, not field strengths, and an electrode gap of 1.00 mm where the paper gives 1.6 mm; the train session reuses the same fields of view at up to seven voltages (82 distinct cells, 311 exposures), where the paper says each cell was tested once (224 cells); the single-pulse session holds 27 cells where the paper averaged 14; the description mentions only single pulses though 33 of 73 files are 60-pulse trains; there are no cell regions, so the paper's cell selection cannot be repeated. The Fluo-4 fluorescence of unpulsed cells declines by 12 to 16% over a recording (8.7 and 7.5% before background subtraction, with the background nearly flat), where the 0 V/cm trace of Fig. 6A rises by about 1% and the Fig. 6B traces are flat; the decline decides fig6a-ca-sustained. It is steepest in the first recording of a field of view: in the single-pulse session it slows with each recording, and in the train session it is 11.4% per minute in the first and 2.0 to 5.4% per minute later, without a steady trend. Field strength and recording order therefore go together in both sessions. A background taken as a low percentile of the cell-free pixels, less affected by dim cells there, leaves the decline and every outcome unchanged.
